open_obligations: Note that Engels et al.'s NSO model takes success as the product of the stepwise Guard win probabilities, so it does not measure error propagation between levels directly.

in.other_title: NSO findings: multi-step oversight beats one step as the capability gap grows
in.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether mistakes compound across levels of recursive reward modeling: whether the mistakes of the narrower agent A(k-1) lead to larger mistakes in training A(k), or can be dampened. Engels et al.'s NSO model plays a series of n games between Guards and Houdinis whose general Elos are spaced Delta_general/n apart, and picks n to maximise the product of the stepwise Guard win probabilities. With it they report that multiple steps of nested oversight can move Guard log odds from -3 to 3 in some regions, with the optimal number of steps growing with the general capability gap (Delta_general) at a fixed Delta_domain; in Houdini-favoured games (Delta_general < Delta_domain), one step of oversight appears optimal. Because each game is set by its Guard's and Houdini's general Elos and overall success is the product of stepwise win probabilities, the model does not show whether mistakes at one level lead to larger mistakes at the next, so neither record bears on the other's claim.
in.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: oversight chained over several levels, in Engels et al.'s Elo-based model of nested scalable oversight and in Leike et al.'s hierarchy of agents trained with recursive reward modeling

in.other_title: C3 critique stage scores below C2 for Qwen2.5-7B on GAOKAO Math
in.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether errors accumulate or are dampened across recursive levels. Wen et al.'s Table 3 compares performance across recursive critique stages and reports values of 43.75 (response), 53.12 (critique), 56.25 (C2) and 54.69 (C3) for GAOKAO Math with Qwen2.5-7B, so the C3 value falls below the C2 value; these are values for a chain of critique stages, and the passage does not show recursive reward model training. Both records concern how results change across successive recursive levels, but neither bears on the other's claim or question: the cited Wen et al. lines pose no question about error accumulation, and Leike et al.'s passage reports no results, so the link is navigation only.
in.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: how errors or performance change across successive recursive levels, in recursive reward modeling (Leike et al.) and across recursive critique stages for Qwen2.5-7B on GAOKAO Math (Wen et al.)

in.other_title: Errors compound up the tree; training on higher-height tasks may be difficult
in.rationale: Leike et al. pose whether mistakes of narrower agents lead to larger mistakes higher up. Wu et al. report that policy errors at lower levels compound at each composition task, leading to large top-level errors, and that training on the full tree did not improve performance; their hierarchy is a fixed summarisation tree, not a chain of assistant agents training stronger agents.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether errors at lower levels of a recursive human-feedback hierarchy compound upward, for recursive book summarisation

text: The authors pose as an important open question whether the mistakes of the narrower agent A(k-1) lead to larger mistakes in training A(k), or whether training can be made self-correcting so small mistakes are dampened (e.g. via ensembles or agents trained to find and counteract mistakes). They argue that if error accumulation can be bounded and reward modeling yields aligned agents, the hierarchy could be argued aligned by analogy to induction.
title: Do errors accumulate across levels of recursive reward modeling?
